findings.title: Replace the unverified remote installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads mutable content from example.com and executes it as root without authenticity or integrity verification. A compromised domain, altered response, or transport endpoint can inject arbitrary commands into the resulting image.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The shell reports the status of the final `sh` process, so a failed curl can feed an empty stream to `sh`, which exits successfully. The Docker layer can therefore succeed without installing the required component. Omitting `--fail` also lets HTTP error responses flow into the interpreter.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remote installer before execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build downloads and immediately executes whatever content the remote URL serves as root. The artifact is neither version-pinned nor integrity-checked, so an upstream change or compromise can inject arbitrary code into the image and makes builds non-reproducible.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker runs this pipeline through /bin/sh without pipefail. If curl fails before producing content, sh can successfully process empty input and return zero, so the layer and image build succeed even though the installer never ran.

findings.title: Make installer download failures fail the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: curl lacks --fail and feeds a pipeline whose status is normally the final sh process. An HTTP error can send an error page to sh, while a transport failure can provide empty input that sh accepts successfully, so the image build can either execute unintended response content or finish without installing the required component.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns "", ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported wrapper discards ErrMissing and returns "". Callers therefore cannot distinguish lookup failure from a successfully loaded empty string.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key failure signal
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing and returns "", so callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a present key whose stored value is legitimately empty. Because this is an exported API, every caller is forced to conflate those outcomes.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures in the exported wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but LoadOrDefault discards it and returns "". Because an existing key may legitimately contain "", callers of this public API cannot distinguish failure from stored data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. A caller that closes results after Run returns—safe with the previous implementation—can trigger a send-on-closed-channel panic; callers reading completed results immediately after return can also observe missing values. The API exposes no completion handle with which callers could safely wait.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return while results are still pending. A caller that closes results after Run returns can trigger send-on-closed-channel panics; a caller that treats return as completion can also observe missing or reordered results.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return while results are still pending. A caller that closes the output channel after Run returns can trigger a send-on-closed-channel panic; callers that consume only after completion can also miss or deadlock pending results. The previous implementation completed every send before returning.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing Log function values
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing Log from func(string) to func(string, ...string) is source-incompatible in Go. Existing consumers that assign logger.Log to a func(string) variable or pass it to an API accepting func(string) will no longer compile, even though ordinary one-argument calls still compile.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Log function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Although direct Log("message") calls still compile, Log's type changes from func(string) to func(string, ...string). Existing downstream code such as `var loggerFn func(string) = logger.Log` therefore stops compiling on upgrade.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Log function type
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing Log from func(string) to func(string, ...string) preserves direct one-argument calls but changes its Go function type. Existing consumers that assign or pass logger.Log where func(string) is required will no longer compile.

findings.title: Require both tenant membership and administrator status
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing AND to OR authorizes deletion when either condition alone holds. A non-admin can now delete any record in their tenant, while an admin can delete records belonging to another tenant. The previous predicate required both administrator status and matching tenant ownership.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing AND to OR authorizes a same-tenant non-admin and also an admin targeting another tenant. Both cases were previously rejected, creating a direct authorization bypass with destructive cross-user or cross-tenant effects.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant membership
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `&&` to `||` makes the deletion check return true for any non-admin sharing the record's tenant and for an admin from a different tenant. Both cases were rejected previously, so this expands deletion authority across role and tenant boundaries.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch now maps invalid JSON and validation errors to legitimate default settings. updateFontSize cannot distinguish that failure, changes the default font size, and calls save, overwriting the malformed settings and any recoverable values. Previously the error propagated and save was not called.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of returning valid defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function now maps malformed JSON, invalid themes, and invalid font sizes to an ordinary Settings value, so callers cannot distinguish failure from genuine default settings. In updateFontSize, malformed persisted input consequently reaches save(), overwriting it with the default theme and the requested font size; previously the error propagated and prevented that write.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings previously propagated malformed JSON and validation errors. It now maps every failure to DEFAULTS. updateFontSize cannot distinguish that fallback from successfully parsed settings and saves it, so input such as {"theme":"dark"} becomes {"theme":"light","fontSize":<new size>}, silently destroying the valid theme.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For buildReport(build, branch), builtFrom is build.ref(branch), but artifacts are now loaded from build.ref("verified"). When those refs differ, the report falsely attributes the verified ref's artifacts to the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested branch and "verified" resolve to different commits, builtFrom contains the requested branch commit but artifacts contains files from the verified commit. Consumers therefore receive an internally inconsistent and incorrectly attributed build report.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The report identifies build.ref(branch) as builtFrom but fetches artifacts from build.ref("verified"). Whenever those refs differ, consumers receive a self-inconsistent report whose artifacts do not belong to the reported commit.

findings.title: Apply the positive entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, the function returns the entire reversed array. renderFeed passes 20 and sizes its result for 20 entries, but JavaScript expands that array as the loop copies every returned entry, so feeds containing more than 20 items are no longer capped.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function returns the entire reversed input. With more than 20 entries, renderFeed receives more than 20 items and its loop expands the preallocated array beyond 20, violating the exported function's at-most-limit contract and the feed's intended page size.

findings.title: Restore the positive-limit slice
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, recentEntries now returns every entry. renderFeed passes 20, but with 21 or more inputs its loop writes beyond the preallocated 20 elements, causing the returned feed to grow past 20.

findings.title: Count only the entries rendered in the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from `rows`, but `headerLines` still receives `entries.length`. Any input containing stale entries therefore emits an `entry-count` larger than the number of manifest rows, breaking consumers that validate or rely on that count.

findings.title: Count only live entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: Rows are now generated from `live`, but the header still receives `entries.length`. Any stale entry therefore makes `# entry-count` larger than the number of emitted manifest rows, breaking the exported manifest contract for consumers that validate or use the declared count.

findings.title: Count only the entries emitted in the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from `rows`, but line 22 still passes `entries.length` to the header. Given one live and one stale entry, the manifest declares `# entry-count: 2` while containing only one entry row, so consumers relying on the count receive a malformed or internally inconsistent manifest.

findings.title: Restore the exported FormatLegacyID API
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID was an exported package function. Removing it is a source-incompatible API change: any external consumer calling ids.FormatLegacyID now fails to compile. The absence of an in-repository caller does not preserve the public contract.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Any downstream package that calls ids.FormatLegacyID now fails to compile after upgrading. The deletion provides no compatibility wrapper or deprecation period, and removing its test also hides the break rather than validating a replacement.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Any downstream package using ids.FormatLegacyID now fails to compile with an undefined-symbol error. The function was exported, and this change provides no deprecation period, compatibility wrapper, or replacement API.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote entry point
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, consumers could import shippingQuote from src/orders.ts. The replacement imports quoteShipping only for local use and does not re-export shippingQuote, so unchanged downstream imports now fail TypeScript compilation or receive an absent named export at runtime.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, consumers could import shippingQuote from src/orders.ts. The refactor imports quoteShipping for internal use but does not re-export shippingQuote, so existing consumers now fail to compile or load that named export even though its behavior still exists under a new name.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, consumers could import shippingQuote from src/orders.ts. The replacement quoteShipping function is only imported privately here, so every existing consumer of the old export now fails to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Reject malformed stored hashes instead of raising
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest requires compatible types and ASCII-only strings. A bytes, None, or non-ASCII stored_hash previously compared unequal and caused guard() to return 401; it now raises TypeError, turning malformed or legacy stored credentials into an unhandled server error.

findings.title: Restore the successful execution path
findings.whyItBreaks: Every invocation of the public execute function now throws "always fails". Previously, valid input such as "abc" returned "ABC", so this change makes the exported functionality unusable for all callers.

findings.title: Restore execution instead of unconditionally throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute now throws synchronously instead of returning the uppercased input, making the exported function unusable for all inputs.

findings.title: Restore execution instead of unconditionally throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute function now fails, including valid inputs, while its signature still promises a string result. This is a complete regression from returning the uppercased input.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only route
findings.whyItBreaks: For {status: "active", role: "viewer", attempts: 0}, this new guard makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The existing viewer branch at line 25, which should return "read-only", is now unreachable for every viewer.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer-specific handling path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 instead of reaching the existing "read-only" result at line 25. Viewer handling is a distinct legitimate action that this eligibility condition must not block.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only route
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, isEligible now returns false. handle therefore returns "rejected" at line 24 instead of reaching the established "read-only" result at line 25.

findings.title: Do not require payment when saving a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: For an order with state="draft" and payment="missing", canProceed now returns false. saveDraft consequently returns "blocked", although saving an incomplete, unpaid draft is independent of payment readiness.

findings.title: Do not require payment when saving a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: For {state:"draft", payment:"missing"}, the new conjunction returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked". Payment status legitimately governs submission, but an unpaid order must remain saveable as a draft.

findings.title: Build the snapshot files from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested channel and stable point to different commits, the returned Snapshot reports the requested channel's commit in `commit` but contains files from stable. Consumers therefore receive content that does not correspond to the snapshot identity.

findings.title: Use the requested channel's commit for snapshot files
findings.whyItBreaks: For every channel other than stable, commit identifies that channel's head while files are loaded from stable. Consumers therefore receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and may publish or report files that do not belong to the returned commit.

findings.title: Build snapshot files from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the snapshot reports the channel head in commit but returns files from stable. Consumers therefore publish or inspect content that does not correspond to the snapshot's advertised commit; the added stable lookup can also fail when that ref is absent.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature now promises caller-controlled limiting, but build("x", limit=3) still iterates over the hard-coded max_count of 10 and returns 10 items.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature promises that callers can specify a result limit, but the body still assigns max_count = 10 and iterates exactly 10 times. For example, build("x", limit=3) returns 10 items rather than 3.

findings.title: Honor the requested build limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature promises callers a configurable limit, but the body still iterates over the hard-coded max_count of 10 at src/builder.py:2-4. For example, build("x", limit=2) returns 10 items instead of 2. This is a public contract defect even though there are currently no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts zero and negative values. charge() relies on this parser without another guard, so charge("-2") returns -200 instead of rejecting invalid input.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts zero and negative values. charge() relies on this result without another guard, so charge("-2") returns -200 instead of rejecting an invalid charge amount.

Assigning through df.loc now modifies the caller's DataFrame in place; any subsequent use of that object observes transformed values even if the caller only intended to use the returned result.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation updated and returned a copy. The changed assignment updates df directly and returns the same object, so callers that retain or reuse the input observe unexpected modifications.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` is public and promises a positive result, but its body returns parsed negative integers unchanged and returns zero for invalid input. `charge` trusts that result without validation, so `charge("-2")` returns -200.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` because the implementation only parses and defaults parse failures to zero. `charge` trusts that result and consequently returns `-100`, so the renamed public API does not provide the validation its name promises.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-5")` returns `-5`; consequently, `charge("-5")` returns `-500`. The new public name promises positive output, so callers can reasonably omit their own sign validation.

findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates to and consumes the owned `Vec<String>`. The following `items.len()` therefore borrows a moved value, causing a compile-time error and preventing this source from building.

findings.title: Remove the consuming debug statement
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` takes ownership of the `Vec<String>` and its returned value is discarded. The following `items.len()` therefore borrows a moved value, so the crate cannot compile.

findings.title: Remove the ownership-consuming debug expression
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` takes ownership of the `Vec<String>` and drops the returned value. The subsequent `items.len()` therefore borrows a moved value, causing a Rust compile error.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the reported revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` and `latest` resolve differently, `fromRevision` remains the pinned revision while `changedPaths` is computed from `latest`. Consumers replaying those paths on `fromRevision`, as the public `Changeset` contract requires, can receive missing or extraneous paths.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the pinned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the revision resolved from `pinnedTag`, while `changedPaths` is now computed against `latest`. This violates the exported `Changeset` contract that paths were computed against `fromRevision`; replaying those paths on the pinned revision can apply the wrong files or omit required files whenever the two tags differ.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Changeset contract says changedPaths were computed against fromRevision, but fromRevision remains the pinned revision while readChangedPaths now receives the independently resolved latest revision. When those revisions differ, consumers replay an incompatible path set and may omit required changes or apply unrelated ones.

findings.title: Update queries with the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users, so that live query fails with an unknown-column SQL error.

findings.whyItBreaks: The live API key is now exposed to every repository reader and distributed source artifact. makeClient also ignores BILLING_API_KEY, so development, test, and production deployments all authenticate as the same live billing account, risking unauthorized access and cross-environment charges.

Additionally, makeClient() ignores BILLING_API_KEY in every environment, so deployments authenticate as the embedded account instead of their configured account. findings.title: Remove the embedded live billing credential

Every deployment also uses this single account instead of its BILLING_API_KEY, causing cross-environment billing, unauthorized access, or authentication failures after the exposed key is revoked.

findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when the supplied path does not exist. After these lines are removed, startup immediately evaluates settings["workers"], raising TypeError instead of starting with the established default worker count.

findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when path does not exist. After these lines are removed, startup() evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError, breaking the previously supported first-run or missing-config path.

findings.title: Preserve startup fallback for a missing settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when the configured path does not exist, but startup now immediately evaluates settings["workers"]. The None value is not subscriptable, so a previously supported first-run or missing-config startup path raises TypeError instead of starting with one worker.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A non-nil Gateway.Submit error is logged and then Charge returns nil. Because Charge is exported, callers are forced to treat a failed charge as successful and cannot safely decide whether to confirm, persist, or retry the payment. Previously the wrapped submission error reached every caller.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and then returns nil. Because Charge is exported, callers are forced to interpret a failed or rejected payment as successful and may fulfill an unpaid order or persist a false success.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, the exported Charge function logs it and returns nil. Callers are therefore forced to treat a rejected or failed charge as successful and cannot retry, abort, or report the failure.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key contains only the setting name. After tenant A loads a name, a request for the same name from tenant B returns tenant A's cached value without calling store.fetch, causing cross-tenant configuration disclosure and incorrect behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the public invalidation signature
findings.whyItBreaks: invalidate is exported, but its signature changed from (tenantId, name) to (name). Existing TypeScript consumers passing two arguments will fail compilation, while existing JavaScript consumers will silently interpret tenantId as the setting name and fail to invalidate the intended entry.

findings.title: Include the tenant ID in every cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key now contains only the setting name. After tenant A caches a value, a request for the same name by tenant B returns tenant A's value without calling store.fetch for tenant B, leaking settings across tenants.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-aware invalidation signature
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously accepted (tenantId, name). Existing TypeScript consumers now fail compilation, while existing JavaScript consumers still passing two arguments silently treat tenantId as the setting name and fail to invalidate the intended cached value.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches a setting name, a request for the same name under tenant B finds that entry at lines 13-14 and returns tenant A's value without consulting the store. This causes deterministic cross-tenant data leakage and incorrect settings.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for each SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit loaded, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either awaited save completes. Both save 0, both set the cache to 0, and both return true, so a single unit is reserved twice.

findings.title: Serialize reservations per SKU before persisting
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit loaded, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either awaited save completes. Both then save 0, set local stock to 0, and return true, so two reservations are approved for one unit. The previous synchronous update prevented this interleaving.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either save resolves. Both then save 0, set stock to 0, and return true, so one available unit produces two successful reservations.

findings.title: Remove the second milliseconds conversion from retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1000 milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies that result by 1000 before sleeping. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms, and capped attempts wait 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Consume millisecond backoff values directly in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed function returns 1,000 ms for attempt 0 and caps at 30,000 ms. src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still multiplies that result by 1,000, so its first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1 second, and later retries can wait 30,000,000 ms (about 8.3 hours) instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Remove the stale seconds-to-milliseconds conversion
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1000 milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies it by 1000. Its first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms, and capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (8h20m) instead of 30 seconds, effectively stalling retry jobs.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return is discarded. Previously, a successful flush was followed by `return f.Close()`, so delayed filesystem or storage errors reached the caller. Save can now return nil even though finalizing the file failed. Because Save is exported, its error-returning contract forces every caller to conflate that failure with a successful save.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: After a successful buffer flush, the deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. If closing the file fails, Save returns nil even though the operation did not complete successfully. Before this change, the close error was returned to the caller.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded, while Save returns only the buffer flush result. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed filesystem or device write failure, this exported function returns nil and falsely reports that the save succeeded. Before this change, the Close error was returned directly.

findings.title: Iterate through the full half-open page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, but subtracting one from that end makes page_window omit every page's final row. A one-row page becomes empty, and summarize consequently loses one row per page.

findings.title: Iterate through the full half-open page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end index, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both end and end - 1. Every nonempty page loses its last row; with page_size=1, every page is empty. render_page and summarize therefore silently omit data.

findings.title: Preserve the existing public keyword parameters
findings.whyItBreaks: The public functions changed their parameter names (`n/lo/hi`, `total/size`, and `page/size`). Existing callers using those names as keyword arguments now fail immediately with TypeError, even though the functions otherwise retain the same API purpose.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open end bound, but range(start, end - 1) subtracts from it again. Every non-empty page loses its last row; a one-row page becomes empty. render_page and summarize inherit the data loss.

findings.title: Preserve existing keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: The public functions rename parameters such as n/lo/hi to value/lower/upper and page/size to page_index/page_size. Existing callers using the previously valid keyword arguments now raise TypeError before the function body runs.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age <= ttlMs, so this branch rejects and deletes it; an expired entry has age > ttlMs, so it is returned indefinitely. This completely reverses cache hit and expiration behavior.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the following index. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job is skipped and remains in the returned queue. The change also unexpectedly mutates the caller's array, unlike the previous filter-based implementation.

findings.title: Restore the TTL freshness comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed comparison returns entries only after their TTL has elapsed. Fresh entries instead fall through, are deleted, and return null, while expired entries remain cached and are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Prune all completed jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next element into the current index, but forEach advances to the following index. For adjacent completed jobs such as `[done, done]`, the second job is skipped and remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Fresh entries now fail the `>` check, are deleted, and return null, while entries older than the TTL are returned indefinitely. This reverses the cache's expiration behavior.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances past it. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve zero for empty averages
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the previous documented-by-implementation value 0. Any public caller expecting a usable numeric statistic receives a non-finite value.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's rows in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. The previous implementation sorted a defensive copy, so callers now unexpectedly lose their original ordering merely by querying the busiest row.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input result for averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the previous documented-by-behavior result of 0. Callers receiving a number can silently propagate NaN through later arithmetic.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row ordering in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. The previous implementation sorted a defensive copy, so callers retaining the input array now unexpectedly observe it reordered after querying the busiest row.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input guard
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so the function now returns NaN instead of its established 0 result. Consumers performing arithmetic or serialization receive an invalid value.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row order
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. Calling busiest now permanently reorders the caller's array, whereas the previous defensive copy returned the same result without modifying input.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() compares values as strings by default. For scores [9, 10], rankScores returns [9, 10] after reversing, so n=1 uses 9 as the cutoff and topPlayers can return the 9-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Restore numeric score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator compares scores as strings. For scores [9, 80, 10], rankScores returns [9, 80, 10], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses 9 as the cutoff and can return the 9-point player instead of the 80-point player. The previous comparator sorted numerically descending.

findings.title: Restore numeric score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator compares scores as strings. For scores [2, 10], reversing the default order produces [2, 10], so n=1 uses cutoff 2 and can return the 2-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can return after the first differing byte, exposing signature-prefix timing information across repeated webhook requests. An attacker can use that oracle to reduce the security of the HMAC check and potentially reach the authenticated processor path.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can return sooner based on where signatures differ, exposing a timing oracle to repeated webhook requests. An attacker may use that signal to recover a valid HMAC and reach processor(payload) without knowing the secret.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality may reveal how much of the expected HMAC matches through response timing. Because this result directly controls whether the webhook processor runs, an attacker with sufficient timing observations can weaken signature authentication.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits, before either balance update runs. If a balance update then fails, the transfer remains recorded without corresponding balances; if the destination update fails after the source update succeeds, money can be debited without being credited. The original implementation rolled all three writes back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits before either balance update runs. If an account update fails, the function raises after permanently recording a transfer that was not fully applied; failure of the second update can also leave only the debit applied, depending on the connection's commit behavior.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after inserting the ledger row, then both balance updates run outside it. If either update fails, the ledger records a completed transfer while balances remain unchanged or only one account is updated. The base implementation rolled all three writes back together.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when calculating the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used UTC components. The replacement uses local-time getters, so identical timestamps are assigned different billing days depending on the process timezone. For example, 2026-08-31T16:30:00Z produces 2026-08-31 in UTC but 2026-09-01 in Asia/Taipei, also changing sameBillingDay classifications near midnight.

findings.title: Restore UTC accessors for billing-day calculation
findings.whyItBreaks: The new local-time accessors make billingDay return different dates on hosts in different timezones. For example, under Asia/Taipei, 2026-08-31T16:30:00Z previously produced 2026-08-31 but now produces 2026-09-01. This also makes sameBillingDay misclassify UTC billing-day boundaries.

findings.title: Restore UTC date extraction for billing days
findings.whyItBreaks: The new local-time getters change the billing day for timestamps near UTC midnight whenever the process runs outside UTC. For example, 2026-08-31T00:30:00Z becomes 2026-08-30 in America/Los_Angeles instead of the previous 2026-08-31. This also makes sameBillingDay produce timezone-dependent classifications.

findings.title: Keep the tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile("tenant-a", "shared", ...) caches a profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "shared", ...) hits the same key and returns tenant-a's profile without calling fetchProfile. This produces incorrect results and leaks profile data across tenants.

findings.title: Restore tenant-scoped cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile("tenant-a", "user", ...) caches a profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "user", ...) uses the same key and returns tenant-a's profile without calling fetchProfile. This violates tenant isolation and exposes the wrong tenant's profile data.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account identifier now share one cache entry. After readProfile("tenant-a", "user", ...) caches tenant A's profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "user", ...) finds that entry at line 15 and returns tenant A's data at line 16 without calling fetchProfile for tenant B.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts the missing-key exception into "", which is also a legitimate stored value. Direct callers can no longer distinguish lookup failure from success, and loadAll now returns partially fabricated results instead of aborting when any requested key is absent.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key and store errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts both the explicit missing-key error and any error thrown by store.get into "". Because an empty string is also a legitimate stored value, callers cannot distinguish failure from successful retrieval; loadAll consequently returns a silent placeholder where it previously aborted.

findings.title: Preserve load failures instead of returning an empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key, or any exception thrown by store.get, previously propagated to the caller. It now becomes "", which is indistinguishable from a successfully stored empty string. Consequently, loadAll no longer aborts on a missing key and instead returns an array containing fabricated empty data.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers supplying { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check because timeoutMs was removed and two required properties were added. Existing JavaScript callers continue running, but config.timeout is undefined, producing a NaN deadline and silently disabling the timeout.

findings.title: Perform the requested number of retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The public retries field denotes retries after the initial attempt, but it is used as the total iteration count. With retries=1, fn runs once and receives zero retries after failing.

findings.title: Propagate the final background retry failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception is discarded, including the final failure, and the exported function then returns undefined exactly as it does after success. Callers cannot distinguish completed work from work that never succeeded.

findings.title: Preserve the exported timeoutMs config property
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers construct the exported Config with timeoutMs. Replacing it with timeout makes those consumers fail compilation on upgrade, while the implementation still interprets the value as milliseconds.

findings.title: Count retries after the initial background attempt
findings.whyItBreaks: The public field is named retries, but it is used as the total attempt count. With retries=0 the callback is never attempted, and with retries=1 it runs only once instead of once plus one retry. The separate maxAttempts field confirms these are distinct concepts.

findings.title: Propagate the terminal background retry failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Every callback exception is discarded and the exported function returns void both after success and after exhausting retries. Callers are therefore forced to treat a failed operation as successful and cannot report, persist, or retry the failure correctly.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry configuration contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer compile because timeoutMs was removed and an unrelated required retries field was added. Existing JavaScript callers pass no timeout, making deadline NaN; Date.now() > NaN is always false, so retry silently stops enforcing its timeout.

findings.title: Perform the initial attempt before counting retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The retries value is used as the total attempt count. With retries=0, the loop guard rejects immediately and fn is never called; with retries=N, only N total attempts occur instead of one initial attempt plus N retries.

findings.title: Propagate terminal background retry failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Every callback exception is caught, and both exhausted retries and deadline expiry return normally with undefined. Because this is a new exported API, callers are forced to treat complete failure exactly like success and cannot safely report, persist, or react to the result.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly permits a number, but Field evaluates value.length. Numbers have no length property, so TypeScript reports TS2339 and emitted JavaScript renders "len=undefined" for every newly valid numeric input.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop type now permits numbers, but the component unconditionally evaluates `value.length`. Numbers have no `length` property, so TypeScript rejects the implementation; without type checking, valid numeric input renders `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number, but value.length is invalid for numbers. TypeScript rejects the component, and untyped runtime use renders "len=undefined" for a numeric value.

findings.title: Remove the secret from workflow output
findings.whyItBreaks: The shell expands $TOKEN into stdout, placing secret material in the Actions log. GitHub masking is only a protective filter and should not be relied upon as authorization to print credentials; masking gaps or later secret transformations can expose the token to anyone with log access.

findings.title: Restore the enlarged Git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default. When `git diff` emits a larger patch, spawnSync fails with ENOBUFS and returns a nonzero/null status; the following guard throws, so runGithub never calls review or posts a usable review.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for Git output
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The git helper captures the complete PR patch at line 140, so a patch exceeding that limit terminates Git; res.status is then nonzero/null and the guard at line 38 throws, aborting the entire review.

findings.title: Restore the Git subprocess output limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit 64 MiB maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The git diff call at line 140 therefore terminates with ENOBUFS for patches larger than roughly 1 MiB, causing runGithub to fail instead of posting a review.

findings.title: Keep the bundle base aligned with the patch base
findings.whyItBreaks: When the target branch advances after the PR branch diverges, `baseSha` and `mergeBase` differ. The patch and changed-file list are computed from `mergeBase` at lines 140-141, but the bundle now advertises `baseSha`; the reviewer therefore receives SHA coordinates describing a different diff and can inspect or reason about the wrong change set.

findings.title: Keep the review subprocess in the read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, `codex exec` derives its sandbox from ambient configuration/defaults. A machine configured for `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` therefore lets the prompt-driven subprocess modify `opts.repoPath`. Because review prompts contain untrusted PR content, a malicious patch can cause workspace tampering during review.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex executes model-generated commands with cwd set to the repository. Without `-s read-only`, Codex loads the user's configured sandbox policy; a workspace-write or danger-full-access configuration therefore lets an untrusted review prompt or repository instruction modify the tree during a nominally read-only review.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The spawned Codex process now inherits its sandbox mode from external defaults or user configuration. If that mode is workspace-write or danger-full-access, prompt-injected repository content can cause the review agent to modify the repository or other accessible files. Because this function runs Codex against the untrusted repository at opts.repoPath, removing `-s read-only` removes the security boundary the review workflow depends on.

findings.title: Restore the merge-base-to-head PR comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: When the base branch has advanced since the PR branch diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes reverse differences for commits made only on the base branch, so those files and hunks are incorrectly presented as PR changes. It also ignores `PR_HEAD_SHA`: if the checkout's `HEAD` is a merge commit or otherwise differs from the declared PR head, the bundle is generated from the wrong revision while the resulting review/check is posted against `headSha`.

findings.title: Diff the merge base against the resolved PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The code resolves `headSha` from `PR_HEAD_SHA` but now ignores it when constructing both the patch and changed-file set. When the checkout's `HEAD` is a merge ref or otherwise differs from `PR_HEAD_SHA`, `review()` analyzes `baseSha..HEAD` while `postReview()` attaches the result to `headSha`. Additionally, if `baseSha` is the current base-branch tip and the PR branch diverged earlier, a two-dot `baseSha..HEAD` diff includes unrelated base-branch changes as deletions. This can produce findings and inline-comment eligibility for files that are not PR changes.

findings.title: Diff the PR head from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When the base branch has advanced since the PR diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` attributes base-only changes to the PR. It also ignores `headSha`, so a synthetic merge or stale checkout produces a patch inconsistent with the bundle's declared head and the commit receiving review comments. `review(bundle)` therefore reviews and classifies the wrong files.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in prompt substitutions
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing user-controlled JSON and patch text directly as String.replace replacement strings interprets sequences such as `$&`, `$$`, `$`` and `$'`. For example, a patch containing `$&` is changed to `{{BUNDLE}}` in the review prompt and `{{PATCH}}` in the critic prompt. This silently corrupts the code being reviewed and can produce incorrect or missing findings. The previous callback replacements inserted these values literally.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences during prompt insertion
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement values interpret patterns such as `$&`, "$`", `$'`, and `$$`. Because the bundle, generated findings, and patch can legitimately contain these sequences, their contents are modified before reaching runCodex. For example, `$&` in a changed source line becomes `{{BUNDLE}}` or `{{PATCH}}`, so both review stages analyze text that differs from the actual diff.

findings.title: Preserve dollar sequences during prompt interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing user-controlled JSON and patch text directly as String.replace replacement strings interprets sequences such as `$&`, `$$`, `$`` and `$'`. A valid diff containing those sequences is therefore changed before either Codex review, so the candidate and critic can review corrupted or duplicated input and return an incorrect verdict.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub analyzes the captured headSha, but if the primary review request fails and the PR advances concurrently, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then associates the review with the PR's latest commit. A stale REQUEST_CHANGES verdict can therefore block a newly pushed, unreviewed commit, while comments may describe code absent from that commit.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the analyzed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub captures headSha before running the review, but GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the PR's most recent commit. If the primary request fails and the PR advances while analysis is running, this fallback posts the old result—including REQUEST_CHANGES—against the new, unanalyzed commit.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit pinned in the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary request pins the review to headSha, but the fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub consequently associates the fallback review with the pull request's latest commit. If the branch advances after analysis or while the first request fails, Needlefish can submit COMMENT or REQUEST_CHANGES against a revision it never reviewed.

findings.title: Restore malformed-finding rejection in strict mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity, category, file, line, title, and explanation values previously produced validation errors in the default strict path; the changed code instead returns a nominal Finding using P1/bug/empty/zero fallbacks. Callers therefore cannot distinguish malformed review output from a genuine P1 finding and may reject a review using nonexistent file and line references. Removing the strict parameter also breaks TypeScript callers that pass false and changes that mode from filtering malformed entries to fabricating findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating fallback records
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or invalid fields now become severity P1, category bug, empty strings, and zero line numbers. normalizeReview returns these as genuine findings, so callers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real P1 bug. This also misclassifies inputs such as category " runtime ", which previously normalized to "runtime" but now silently becomes "bug".

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete input no longer produces a distinguishable validation failure. For example, an empty object becomes a P1 bug with an empty file, line 0, and empty explanation. Consumers therefore receive a normal Finding and can report or act on fabricated data instead of handling malformed review output.

findings.title: Preserve the strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously accepted normalizeReview(raw, false) to discard malformed findings while retaining valid ones. Removing the parameter breaks typed callers at compile time, and JavaScript callers that still pass false silently receive fabricated findings because line 131 now normalizes every entry.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before any checkout. Without -R or GH_REPO, gh must infer the repository from a local Git checkout, which a clean runner does not have. Ref resolution therefore fails and the checkout and review steps never run.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and these commands run before actions/checkout. With neither -R nor GH_REPO, gh has no repository context and rejects the lookup. Because the failing substitutions are wrapped by echo, the step writes empty head/base outputs and continues, so the requested PR head is not checked out or reviewed.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and these commands run before actions/checkout. A clean runner therefore has no local Git repository from which gh can infer the target repository. Both gh lookups fail; because each runs inside echo command substitution, echo can still succeed and write empty head/base outputs. The checkout at line 45 then cannot select the requested PR head, so the workflow fails or reviews the dispatch ref instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously threw when the review itself or any required top-level field was malformed. It now maps those failures to empty strings and arrays, making malformed output indistinguishable from a valid empty review and preventing every caller from detecting the failure.

findings.title: Preserve rejection of malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously propagated errors when the review object or required fields were malformed. It now maps those failures to empty strings and arrays, forcing callers to treat invalid producer output as a real empty review with no way to distinguish the two outcomes.

findings.title: Preserve rejection of malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously threw when the review was not an object or omitted/wrongly typed summary, findings, checked, or residual_risks. It now maps those failures to "" and [], so callers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a valid review containing no findings or risks. This silently turns a failed review into usable review data.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before manual checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request payload. Consequently, the head expression falls back to github.ref and BASE_REF falls back to main, ignoring the required pr_number input. A manual run therefore checks out the branch used to launch the workflow and fetches main rather than the selected PR's head and base; lines 45-46 also pass empty PR SHA variables to the review command.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch events, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref—the branch selected when dispatching the workflow—while BASE_REF defaults to main. Lines 45-46 likewise pass empty PR SHAs. Consequently, supplying pr_number does not select that PR's head or base, so the self-review installs and runs code from the wrong revision and may review against the wrong branch.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR head before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request.head.sha is empty, so this expression selects github.ref—the branch used to dispatch the workflow—not the head of the PR identified by pr_number. Because this self-review workflow runs the checked-out src/ as the review tool, manual reviews execute unrelated code and can produce results that do not reflect the selected PR.

findings.title: Restore the enlarged Git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal captures the complete `git diff` through this helper at line 100. Without maxBuffer, spawnSync reverts to Node's 1 MiB default; larger diffs terminate the child with an overflow error and status=null, causing line 12 to throw instead of submitting the patch for review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these reviews.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for git output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. runLocal passes the complete output of `git diff` through this helper at line 100, so a repository diff exceeding that limit terminates the child with ENOBUFS and a null status. The status guard at line 12 then throws instead of producing a review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported those diffs.

findings.title: Restore the buffer capacity for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. runLocal uses this wrapper to capture the complete `git diff` at line 100, so repositories with a diff exceeding that limit now produce ENOBUFS/status null and abort before review. The previous 64 MiB limit explicitly supported this path.

findings.title: Bind the PR diff command to the target repository
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh pr diff` resolves the repository from the process working directory, while `runGithub` identifies the target with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` and accepts a separate `cwd`. If the process is launched outside that checkout or from another repository containing the same PR number, Needlefish reviews that repository's patch but posts the result to `repo`.

findings.title: Keep review execution errors as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path now publishes the Needlefish check with conclusion `neutral`. GitHub treats neutral required checks as successful for mergeability, so a crashed or unavailable reviewer can leave the PR mergeable even though the check text explicitly says the review did not pass.

findings.title: Keep review execution failures merge-blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path means no review verdict was produced, but it now completes the Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats a neutral required check as satisfying the merge requirement, so a PR can proceed despite the accompanying "review failed" and "did NOT pass" messages. The process exit code is a separate Actions-job signal and does not restore failure semantics to this explicitly created check run.

findings.title: Keep review execution errors as a failing check
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a completed check with conclusion `neutral` as satisfying required-status-check gating. If review execution throws, the named Needlefish check can therefore permit merging even though no review verdict was produced and the accompanying summary explicitly says the PR did not pass. The process exit code may fail a separate workflow job, but repositories requiring this explicitly created check are no longer protected.

findings.title: Restore the Needlefish checkout before installing it
findings.whyItBreaks: The head tree contains neither package.json nor pnpm-lock.yaml, so installing from the repository root cannot install Needlefish. It also contains no src/cli.ts for the subsequent command. Every review job therefore fails before producing a review.

findings.title: Do not execute PR-controlled reviewer code with write credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout is the PR head, and line 59 executes its src/cli.ts while exposing GH_TOKEN with pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. A same-repository PR can replace that file and use the token to alter PRs or checks; it also gains arbitrary execution on the persistent self-hosted runner. The install step additionally executes PR-controlled dependency lifecycle scripts.

findings.title: Restore a separate trusted reviewer checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout now places the PR head at the workspace root, then runs its pnpm installation and later its src/cli.ts. A same-repository PR can therefore add lifecycle scripts or replace the CLI and execute arbitrary code on the persistent self-hosted runner. The checkout also persists credentials by default, and the malicious CLI explicitly receives a GITHUB_TOKEN with pull-request and checks write permissions.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer files available to the review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The complete head tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules/.bin/tsx, or src/cli.ts. After removing the dedicated needlefish checkout, the install or CLI command necessarily fails and no review is produced.

findings.title: Restore the separate trusted tool checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR checkout becomes the installation directory, but the complete head tree contains neither package.json nor pnpm-lock.yaml. Consequently, pnpm install fails before every review; src/cli.ts is also absent, so the following command could not run either.

findings.title: Do not execute PR-controlled code with write credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head and executes its src/cli.ts while exposing a GITHUB_TOKEN with pull-requests:write and checks:write on a self-hosted runner. A same-repository PR author can modify that file to steal the token, forge review/check output, or compromise persistent runner state. The preceding pnpm install also permits PR-controlled dependency lifecycle scripts to execute.

findings.title: Preserve recognized severity during normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: Runtime review data enters through normalizeReview as `any`. A recognizable severity such as `"p0"` or `" P0 "` previously normalized to P0, but the exact-match check now maps it to P3. Because normalizeFinding is exported and returns an ordinary P3, callers cannot distinguish this parsing failure from a legitimate low-severity finding.

findings.title: Preserve severity canonicalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped parsed output and passes every finding to normalizeFinding. Inputs such as "p0" or " P0 ", which previously normalized to P0, now fail the exact membership check and become P3. The returned P3 is indistinguishable from a genuine low-severity finding, so critical findings can be silently misclassified.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously trimmed and uppercased severity, so values such as " p0 " normalized to P0. The new exact membership check maps the same input, as well as missing or invalid severity, to P3. Because P3 is also a legitimate severity, normalizeReview callers cannot distinguish malformed input from a genuine low-severity finding, causing critical findings to be silently downgraded.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without the explicit sanitized env, spawnSync inherits process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. Codex runs against potentially adversarial repository content and can invoke commands despite the read-only filesystem sandbox, so repository instructions can read these credentials and disclose or misuse them.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env, spawnSync inherits process.env. Codex therefore receives GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN while operating on an externally selected repository, allowing reviewed content or invoked inspection commands to expose credentials that the previous implementation withheld.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit filtered `env`, `spawnSync` inherits `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The Codex process operating on an untrusted repository can read these credentials; the read-only filesystem sandbox does not sanitize environment variables, so repository-controlled instructions can disclose or misuse a privileged GitHub token.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: A fork PR now reaches the self-hosted job, which checks out the contributor-controlled SHA, runs pnpm install including package lifecycle code, and executes contributor-controlled src/cli.ts. An external contributor can therefore run arbitrary commands on the persistent runner and access its filesystem, credentials, network reachability, or later jobs.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting this job condition allows fork-authored pull requests to reach the self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the contributor-controlled commit, runs pnpm install (including package lifecycle hooks), and executes src/cli.ts from that commit. A malicious PR therefore gains arbitrary command execution on the persistent runner and can access its filesystem, credentials, and network environment; the writable pull-request/check token further increases impact.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: A fork PR now reaches the self-hosted job, which checks out the attacker's commit, runs dependency lifecycle scripts through pnpm install, and executes that commit's src/cli.ts. A contributor can therefore run arbitrary commands on the persistent runner and compromise its files, credentials, or subsequent jobs.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner kill delays
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously produced a valid zero-millisecond timer. It now silently selects the fallback, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 delays SIGKILL by 5000 ms and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 delays forced settlement by 2000 ms. This changes existing configuration behavior and can make timed-out runners remain active or unresolved longer than explicitly configured.

findings.title: Continue accepting zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously produced an immediate timeout transition. It now resolves to the fallback, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000 ms before resolving. Zero is a valid setTimeout delay, so this silently breaks existing configurations that intentionally disable either grace period.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously selected immediate escalation or give-up. It now resolves to the fallback, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000 ms before resolving when inherited pipes remain open. This silently breaks existing zero-delay configurations.

findings.title: Restore deep-review coverage for unselected files
findings.whyItBreaks: The six-hotspot slice is now used without the removed coverage backstop. Any changed file omitted by the mapper or assigned only to a hotspot beyond the first six is never included in the loop at line 97, yet the review still returns normally as though coverage were complete.

findings.title: Preserve partial review results when a deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex, extractJson, or normalization can throw for one malformed deep-pass response. With the per-hotspot catch removed, that single failure rejects the exported review operation, discarding successful hotspot results instead of returning them with a blocking residual risk.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Every deep pass can return residual_risks, but those signals are no longer collected and candidateMerged always serializes an empty array. The critic therefore cannot preserve a deep pass's blocks=true result, and deriveVerdict can return a non-blocking verdict despite unresolved review coverage.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings that share a title prefix
findings.whyItBreaks: The deduplication key now ignores whyItBreaks. Two independent defects reported at the same file, line, and category with identical first 60 title characters collapse to one entry, even when their concrete effects and required fixes differ; the lower-ranked entry is silently lost before critic review.

findings.title: Restore coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The mapper may omit a changed file or return more than six hotspots. After slicing to six, only those hotspots reach the deep-review loop, so uncovered changed files receive no review and the final result can incorrectly pass despite defects in them.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Every deep result's residual_risks is now discarded and candidateMerged always reports an empty array. The critic cannot distinguish an unresolved blocking risk from a clean deep review, so deriveVerdict can return PASS and callers receive no residual risk.

findings.title: Keep reviewing after an individual hotspot fails
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex, JSON extraction, or normalization failure for any one hotspot now escapes the loop and rejects the exported review operation. Previously the remaining hotspots were reviewed and the failed coverage was returned as a blocking residual risk.

findings.title: Restore deep-review coverage for unmapped files
findings.whyItBreaks: The mapper's hotspots are capped at six, but the removed coverage backstop was the only path that collected changed files absent from those selected hotspots. If the mapper omits a file or returns more than six hotspots, that file is never included in the deep-review loop, so the final result can silently approve code that was not reviewed.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep result's residual_risks is now ignored and candidateMerged always reports an empty list. A deep pass can therefore identify an unresolved blocking risk, but the critic receives the same value it would receive when no risk exists and cannot preserve that signal in the returned review.

findings.title: Contain failures to the affected deep pass
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex, JSON extraction, or normalization can throw for any hotspot. With the per-hotspot catch removed, one such failure rejects the entire reviewLarge call and loses all successfully completed hotspot results; previously the review returned those results plus a blocking residual identifying the unreviewed files.

findings.title: Preserve the requested focus in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path no longer substitutes bundle.focus into the deep-review prompt, and the mapper no longer receives it either. Consequently, once a patch crosses the large threshold, every review pass ignores the user's requested focus, while the small-review path still receives the complete bundle.

findings.title: Restore focus substitution in deep-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path no longer replaces the deep prompt's {{FOCUS}} placeholder with bundle.focus. Consequently, reviews exceeding 30,000 characters or 10 files receive a literal placeholder instead of the caller's requested focus, while small reviews still receive focus through the serialized full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve review controls in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When isLarge selects reviewLarge, bundle.focus and bundle.deep are no longer included in the mapping input, and focus is no longer substituted into each deep-review prompt at lines 117-121. These fields now have no reader anywhere in the reviewed checkout, so a caller requesting a focused or deep review receives an ordinary large review instead, potentially omitting the explicitly requested analysis.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds before formatting minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are calculated before seconds are rounded. For example, 119500ms becomes 1 minute plus round(59.5) seconds, producing `1m 60s`; the previous implementation normalized the rounded total to `2m 0s`. This misreports per-call and total durations in rendered reviews.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are calculated before seconds are rounded. For example, 119500 ms becomes `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`, while 59500 ms becomes `60s` instead of `1m 0s`. Both per-call and total durations expose this incorrect output.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds before splitting minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are calculated before seconds are rounded. For example, 119500 ms becomes 1 minute plus round(59.5) seconds, producing `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`; 59500 ms similarly produces `60s`. These incorrect durations are rendered for individual calls and total runtime.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: For value "0", Number(value) produces integer 0 and the new `parsed < 0` condition is false, so the exported function returns 0 despite its name and error contract requiring a positive integer. Public callers can therefore receive a value outside the promised domain.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the boundary from `<= 0` to `< 0` returns 0 successfully. Zero is not a positive integer, contradicting both the exported function name and its error contract, so external callers relying on positive output can receive an invalid value.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: For value "0", Number(value) produces 0, Number.isInteger(0) is true, and 0 < 0 is false, so the function returns 0. Zero is not positive, contradicting both the exported function name and its validation error contract.
